title: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter

questions.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.q: The stopping potential in a photoelectric experiment depends on:
options: The intensity of the incident light
The frequency of the incident light
questions.solution:
$eV_0 = K_{\max} = h\nu - \phi$, so the stopping potential depends on the **frequency** of the light and on the metal's work function — never on the intensity.

A graph of $V_0$ against $\nu$ is a straight line of slope $\dfrac{h}{e}$, and that slope comes out the **same for every metal**, which is what shows $h$ to be a universal constant.

questions.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.q: The threshold frequency of a metal is $\nu_0$. Photoelectrons are emitted only when the incident frequency $\nu$ satisfies:
questions.solution:
Emission requires $h\nu > \phi = h\nu_0$, that is $\mathbf{\nu > \nu_0}$.

Below the threshold **no electrons are emitted at all**, however intense the light or however long it shines — because one electron absorbs one whole photon, and a photon below threshold simply lacks the energy to free it.

This is the observation the wave theory could not explain, since on that picture energy would accumulate until emission occurred.

questions.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.q: The de Broglie wavelength of a particle of mass $m$ moving with velocity $v$ is:
questions.solution:
$\lambda = \mathbf{\dfrac{h}{mv}} = \dfrac{h}{p}$.

Because $h$ is so small, an everyday object has an utterly unobservable wavelength — a cricket ball's is around $10^{-34}\ \text{m}$.

An electron accelerated through a few tens of volts, however, has $\lambda$ of about an ångström, comparable to atomic spacing, which is exactly why electrons diffract off crystals and why the electron microscope works.

questions.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.q: Increasing the intensity of light above the threshold frequency increases:
options: The maximum kinetic energy of photoelectrons
questions.solution:
Greater intensity means **more photons per second**, so more electrons are emitted per second and the **photoelectric current** rises.

Each electron still absorbs exactly one photon of the same energy, so $K_{\max}$ is unchanged.

The saturation current is proportional to intensity; the stopping potential is not.

questions.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.solution:
Davisson and Germer scattered electrons from a nickel crystal and found a **diffraction pattern** — intensity maxima at particular angles, exactly as X-rays give.

Diffraction is a wave phenomenon, so this confirmed de Broglie's hypothesis that **electrons behave as waves**, and the measured wavelength agreed with $\lambda = h/p$.

Taken together with the photoelectric effect, which shows light behaving as particles, it establishes **wave-particle duality** as a property of matter and radiation alike.

questions.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.q: The momentum of a photon of wavelength $\lambda$ is:
options: Zero, since a photon has no mass
questions.solution:
$p = \mathbf{\dfrac{h}{\lambda}} = \dfrac{E}{c}$.

A photon has **zero rest mass but non-zero momentum** — which is not a contradiction, because the relation $p = mv$ does not apply to a massless particle. The correct relation is $E^{2} = p^{2}c^{2} + m_0^{2}c^{4}$, which for $m_0 = 0$ gives $E = pc$.

That photons carry momentum is confirmed by radiation pressure and by the Compton effect.

questions.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.q: The work function of a metal is the:
options: Minimum energy needed to free an electron from the metal surface
Kinetic energy of the emitted electron
questions.solution:
The work function $\phi$ is the **minimum energy** required to remove an electron from the metal surface.

It is a property of the **metal**, not of the light. Caesium has a low work function of about $2.1\ \text{eV}$ and so responds to visible light, which is why it is used in photocells; platinum's is around $5.6\ \text{eV}$ and needs ultraviolet.

It relates to the threshold frequency by $\phi = h\nu_0$.

questions.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
options: Delayed by hours for weak light
questions.solution:
Emission is **instantaneous**, occurring within about $10^{-9}\ \text{s}$ of the light arriving, even for very faint light.

This is one of the observations that destroyed the wave theory. On that picture an electron would have to **accumulate** energy from the spreading wavefront, and the calculated delay for weak light runs to **hours**.

The photon picture explains it immediately: one electron absorbs one whole photon in a single event, so there is nothing to wait for.

questions.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.q: For particles of the same kinetic energy, which has the longest de Broglie wavelength?
questions.solution:
$\lambda = \dfrac{h}{p} = \dfrac{h}{\sqrt{2mK}}$, so at fixed kinetic energy $\lambda \propto \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{m}}$.

The **lightest** particle has the longest wavelength, and of these the **electron** is by far the lightest — about 1836 times lighter than a proton.

This is also why electron microscopes use electrons: a short wavelength gives fine resolution, and accelerating them makes $\lambda$ shorter still.

questions.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.q: Light of energy $6\ \text{eV}$ falls on a metal of work function $2.5\ \text{eV}$. Find the maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons, in electronvolts.
questions.solution:
$K_{\max} = h\nu - \phi = 6 - 2.5 = \mathbf{3.5\ \text{eV}}$.

The stopping potential needed to halt these electrons is therefore $3.5\ \text{V}$.

questions.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.q: The threshold wavelength for a metal surface whose photoelectric work function is 3.313 eV, in nanometres :
questions.solution:
$\lambda_0 = \dfrac{hc}{\phi_0} = \dfrac{6.626\times10^{-34} \times 3\times10^{8}}{3.313 \times 1.6\times10^{-19}} = \dfrac{1.988\times10^{-25}}{5.301\times10^{-19}} = 3.75\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{m}$

$\lambda_0 = \mathbf{375\ nm}$ (3750 Å), in the near ultraviolet.

questions.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.q: An electron is accelerated through $100\ \text{V}$. Using $\lambda = \dfrac{12.27}{\sqrt{V}}\ \text{Å}$, find its de Broglie wavelength in ångström, to two decimal places.
questions.solution:
$\sqrt{100} = 10$

$\lambda = \dfrac{12.27}{10} = \mathbf{1.23\ \text{Å}}$

Comparable to atomic spacing in a crystal, which is why such electrons are diffracted by one.

questions.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.q: How many photons per second emanate from a 50 mW laser of 640 nm ? Give the answer in units of $10^{17}$.
questions.solution:
Energy of one photon: $E = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda} = \dfrac{6.626\times10^{-34} \times 3\times10^{8}}{640\times10^{-9}} = 3.11\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm{J}$

$N = \dfrac{P}{E} = \dfrac{0.05}{3.11\times10^{-19}} = 1.61\times10^{17}$ photons per second. Answer: $\mathbf{1.61}$.

questions.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.q: A radiation of wavelength 300 nm is incident on calcium surface. Will photoelectrons be observed ? Justify your answer. (Work function of calcium = 3.20 eV) Answer Yes or No.
questions.solution:
$E = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda} = \dfrac{6.626\times10^{-34} \times 3\times10^{8}}{300\times10^{-9} \times 1.6\times10^{-19}} = 4.14\ \mathrm{eV}$

$4.14\ \mathrm{eV} > 3.20\ \mathrm{eV}$, so **Yes**: photoelectrons are emitted, with a maximum kinetic energy of about $0.94$ eV.

questions.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.q: State the laws of the photoelectric effect. Explain in detail why the classical wave theory fails to account for them, write Einstein's photoelectric equation, and explain how a graph of stopping potential against frequency yields Planck's constant and the work function.
questions.solution:
**The experimental laws.**

1. Emission is **instantaneous** — within about $10^{-9}\ \text{s}$ — however faint the light.
2. There is a **threshold frequency** $\nu_0$ below which no emission occurs at all, whatever the intensity or duration.
3. The **maximum kinetic energy** of the emitted electrons depends on the **frequency** of the light and on the metal, and is **completely independent of the intensity**.
4. The **number** of electrons emitted per second, and so the photoelectric current, is proportional to the **intensity**.

**Why the wave theory fails.** On the classical picture, light is a wave whose energy is spread continuously over the wavefront and carried by the intensity. Each of the four laws contradicts it, and the contradictions are not marginal.

**Against law 1.** An electron would have to **accumulate** energy from the wave until it had enough to escape. For light faint enough, the calculation gives delays of **hours**. Experiment finds no measurable delay whatever.

**Against law 2.** There should be **no threshold at all**. Light of any frequency, given enough intensity or enough time, ought eventually to deliver the required energy. Yet below $\nu_0$ nothing is emitted however long one waits — which on the wave picture is inexplicable rather than merely surprising.

**Against law 3.** A more intense wave carries more energy per unit area, so it should eject **faster** electrons. Instead it ejects **more** electrons at exactly the same maximum speed.

**The deepest problem** is that the wave theory makes everything depend on **intensity**, and the experiment makes the crucial things depend on **frequency**. It is not that the theory is quantitatively off; it identifies the wrong variable.

**Einstein's explanation (1905).** Light is absorbed in discrete quanta — **photons** — each of energy $h\nu$. One electron absorbs **one whole photon**, all at once, in a single event.

Part of that energy frees the electron from the metal, the **work function** $\phi$; the rest appears as kinetic energy:

$\boxed{h\nu = \phi + K_{\max}}$

or $K_{\max} = h\nu - \phi = h\nu - h\nu_0 = h(\nu - \nu_0)$.

Every law now follows without further assumption:

- **One photon, one electron, one event** — so emission is instantaneous, with nothing to accumulate.
- If $h\nu < \phi$, **no single photon** can free an electron, and a million such photons are a million individually inadequate attempts, not one adequate one. Hence the threshold, $\nu_0 = \phi/h$.
- $K_{\max}$ contains $\nu$ and does not contain the intensity.
- Greater intensity is simply **more photons**, hence more electrons.

**Obtaining $h$ and $\phi$ from a graph.**

Apply a reverse potential just sufficient to stop the fastest electrons. Then $eV_0 = K_{\max}$, so

$eV_0 = h\nu - \phi$

$V_0 = \left(\dfrac{h}{e}\right)\nu - \dfrac{\phi}{e}$

This is $y = mx + c$. Measure $V_0$ at several frequencies and plot $V_0$ against $\nu$. The graph is a **straight line**, and three quantities can be read from it:

**Slope** $= \dfrac{h}{e}$, so $h = e \times \text{slope}$.

**Intercept on the $\nu$ axis** $= \nu_0$, the threshold frequency.

**Intercept on the $V_0$ axis** $= -\dfrac{\phi}{e}$, giving the work function.

**The decisive feature of this graph.** Repeat the experiment with a **different metal** and the line shifts — a different threshold, a different intercept — but the **slope is identical**.

That is what proves $h$ is a **universal constant of nature** and not a property of the particular surface. A result that depended on the metal would say something about caesium; a result that does not says something about the world.

Millikan spent ten years attempting to **disprove** Einstein's equation, which he considered unjustified, and ended by confirming it to high precision and measuring $h$ by exactly this method. It is among the better illustrations of how a theory earns acceptance — not by its author's advocacy, but by surviving the efforts of someone determined to break it.
